cards.left-cwe-20.say: Input the code doesn't check can reach parts of it that trust it, and most other attacks start this way.

cards.left-cwe-22.say: An attacker can read or write files outside the folder the code meant to use, such as configuration or keys.

cards.left-cwe-74.say: An attacker can inject commands or markup into output another part of the system trusts.

cards.left-cwe-77.say: An attacker can run commands on the server.

cards.left-cwe-78.say: An attacker can run operating system commands on the server.

cards.left-cwe-79.say: An attacker can run script in a user's browser and act as that user, reading their session too.

cards.left-cwe-89.say: An attacker can read, change or delete database records by injecting queries.

cards.left-cwe-93.say: An attacker can inject extra headers or lines into a response, splitting it or setting cookies.

cards.left-cwe-94.say: An attacker can make the application run code of their choosing.

cards.left-cwe-113.say: An attacker can inject extra headers into a response, splitting it or setting cookies.

cards.left-cwe-116.say: The code doesn't escape output for where it lands, so crafted input can change what a browser or parser does.

cards.left-cwe-125.say: A crafted input can make the software read memory it shouldn't, leaking data or crashing it.

cards.left-cwe-180.say: The code checks input before normalising it, so a crafted value can pass the check and act as something else.

cards.left-cwe-183.say: An allow list admits more than intended, letting through values it was meant to stop.

cards.left-cwe-190.say: A number can overflow and corrupt memory or get past a size check.

cards.left-cwe-200.say: Someone without permission can see information meant to stay private.

cards.left-cwe-201.say: The code can send sensitive data where it shouldn't go, such as in a response or a request to another site.

cards.left-cwe-248.say: The code doesn't catch an unexpected error, so a crafted request can crash the service.

cards.left-cwe-285.say: A user can reach data or actions their role shouldn't allow.

cards.left-cwe-287.say: An attacker can get past sign-in and act as another user.

cards.left-cwe-295.say: The code doesn't check a certificate properly, so someone can intercept or alter the traffic.

cards.left-cwe-345.say: The code trusts data without checking where it came from, so it can accept a forged value.

cards.left-cwe-346.say: The code doesn't check where a request came from, so another site can act on a user's behalf.

cards.left-cwe-347.say: The code doesn't check a signature properly, so it can accept forged data as genuine.

cards.left-cwe-352.say: Another site can make a signed-in user's browser perform actions without their knowledge.

cards.left-cwe-367.say: The state can change between a check and the action it guards, so an attacker can slip past the check.

cards.left-cwe-400.say: A crafted request can use enough resources to slow or stop the service.

cards.left-cwe-407.say: A crafted input can make an algorithm run far longer than expected, slowing or stopping the service.

cards.left-cwe-416.say: The code uses memory after freeing it, so it can crash or let an attacker run code.

cards.left-cwe-434.say: An attacker can upload a file the server will run or serve as trusted content.

cards.left-cwe-436.say: Two parts of the system read the same input differently, so an attacker can slip something past one of them.

cards.left-cwe-444.say: A request can slip past a proxy unchecked and reach the application, or poison other users' responses.

cards.left-cwe-476.say: A missing value can crash the software.

cards.left-cwe-502.say: The code turns untrusted data back into objects, so an attacker can run code.

cards.left-cwe-521.say: The system accepts weak passwords, so accounts are easier to guess.

cards.left-cwe-524.say: A cache can keep sensitive data and serve it to the wrong person.

cards.left-cwe-525.say: A browser or shared cache can keep sensitive pages for another user to see.

cards.left-cwe-601.say: A link on a trusted site can send users on to an attacker's site and make phishing convincing.

cards.left-cwe-611.say: A crafted document can make the parser read local files or reach internal services.

cards.left-cwe-613.say: Sessions stay valid longer than they should, so a stolen one keeps working.

cards.left-cwe-636.say: A failure leaves the system open when it should close, so an error becomes a way in.

cards.left-cwe-639.say: A user can reach another user's records by changing an identifier in a request.

cards.left-cwe-668.say: People who shouldn't reach a resource can reach it.

cards.left-cwe-693.say: An attacker can get around a protection the code relies on.

cards.left-cwe-705.say: An error sends the code down an unexpected path and can leave it in an unsafe state.

cards.left-cwe-754.say: The code doesn't handle an unusual condition, so the service can crash or end up in an unsafe state.

cards.left-cwe-755.say: The code doesn't handle an error properly, so the service can crash or end up in an unsafe state.

cards.left-cwe-770.say: Nothing limits how much a request can allocate, so a crafted one can exhaust memory and stop the service.

cards.left-cwe-776.say: A crafted document can expand until it fills memory and stops the service.

cards.left-cwe-787.say: A crafted input can make the software write outside its memory and let an attacker run code.

cards.left-cwe-798.say: The code holds a credential, so anyone who can read the code can use it.

cards.left-cwe-834.say: Nothing bounds how often a loop runs, so a crafted input can stall the service.

cards.left-cwe-835.say: A crafted input can send the code into a loop it never leaves, stalling the service.

cards.left-cwe-915.say: A request can set fields it shouldn't, such as a user's role.

cards.left-cwe-918.say: An attacker can make the server send requests to internal systems it can reach and they can't.

cards.left-cwe-922.say: The system stores sensitive data where others can read it.

cards.left-cwe-940.say: The code doesn't check where a message came from, so it can accept a forged one.

cards.left-cwe-59.say: An attacker can use a link to make the code read or write a file it didn't mean to.

cards.left-cwe-184.say: A deny list misses a dangerous value, so it gets through the check meant to stop it.

cards.left-cwe-471.say: An attacker can change data the code relies on staying fixed.

cards.left-cwe-501.say: The code mixes trusted and untrusted data, so it can treat input as if the system had vouched for it.

cards.left-cwe-665.say: The code uses something before setting it up properly, so it can crash or end up in an unsafe state.

cards.left-cwe-783.say: An operator applies in an unexpected order, so a check can pass when it should fail.

cards.left-cwe-789.say: A crafted input can make the software reserve a huge amount of memory and stop the service.

cards.left-cwe-1284.say: The code doesn't check a size or index in the input, so a crafted value can crash or stall the software.

cards.left-cwe-1285.say: The code doesn't check an index in the input, so a crafted value can read or change the wrong data.

cards.left-cwe-1289.say: The code doesn't handle an unusual input that looks valid, so a crafted value can crash the software or get past a check.

cards.left-cwe-1321.say: An attacker can change how shared objects in the application behave, so checks can fail open or their code can run.

cards.left-cwe-1333.say: A crafted input can make a pattern match run for a very long time, stalling the service.

cards.fix-cwe-20.say: Check the input against what the code expects before using it, and refuse anything else.

cards.fix-cwe-22.say: Build the file path from an allowed name or an identifier, and refuse any path that leaves the intended folder.

cards.fix-cwe-78.say: Pass arguments to the command as a list, never through a shell, and never build the command from input.

cards.fix-cwe-79.say: Escape the value for where it lands in the page, or clean it with a library such as DOMPurify before inserting it as HTML.

cards.fix-cwe-89.say: Use parameterised queries, and never build a query by joining input into the text.

cards.fix-cwe-94.say: Remove the code that runs text as code, or limit it to a fixed set of values.

cards.fix-cwe-200.say: Remove the sensitive value from what the code returns or logs.

cards.fix-cwe-295.say: Turn certificate checking back on, and trust only the certificates the service needs.

cards.fix-cwe-312.say: Encrypt the value where it's stored, or stop storing it.

cards.fix-cwe-319.say: Send the data over an encrypted connection only.

cards.fix-cwe-327.say: Replace the weak algorithm with a current one, such as AES-GCM for encryption or SHA-256 for hashing.

cards.fix-cwe-328.say: Replace the weak hash with a current one, and use a password hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2 for passwords.

cards.fix-cwe-330.say: Use a cryptographically secure random source, such as crypto.randomBytes or the secrets module.

cards.fix-cwe-352.say: Require an anti-forgery token or a same-site cookie on every request that changes state.

cards.fix-cwe-502.say: Parse untrusted data with a format that can't create objects, such as JSON, or check its signature first.

cards.fix-cwe-532.say: Remove the sensitive value from the log line, or mask it.

cards.fix-cwe-601.say: Redirect only to paths on this site or to an allowed list of addresses.

cards.fix-cwe-611.say: Parse XML with external entities and DTDs turned off, and in Python use the defusedxml package in place of the xml modules.

cards.fix-cwe-614.say: Set the Secure flag on the cookie so the browser sends it over encrypted connections only.

cards.fix-cwe-776.say: Parse XML with entity expansion limited or turned off.

cards.fix-cwe-798.say: Revoke and reissue the credential, then load it from the environment or a secret store, and remove it from the code and its history.

cards.fix-cwe-918.say: Allow outbound requests only to known addresses, and refuse internal and link-local ones.

cards.fix-cwe-1004.say: Set the HttpOnly flag on the cookie so scripts in the page can't read it.

cards.fix-cwe-1333.say: Rewrite the pattern so it can't backtrack without bound, or limit the length of the input it runs on.

say.one: This scan didn't record which package brings it in.
say.many: This scan didn't record which package brings each one in.

say.one: No published version of <name> fixes this, so reduce what reaches it or replace it.
say.many: No published version of <name> fixes these, so reduce what reaches it or replace it.

cards.bring-copies.say: Bring <which> copies of <name>, <versions>, up to <target> to fix <fixes>.

cards.breaking.say: Moving from <from> to <target> is a breaking step under semantic versioning, so check the release notes before shipping it.

cards.unknown-several.say: Another package probably brings one of them in. Upgrade the repository's own dependency, and upgrade or override the package that brings in the other.

cards.unknown-several-why.say: Another package probably brings one of them in, and <why> shows which. Upgrade the repository's own dependency, and upgrade or override the package that brings in the other.

cards.unknown-one-why.say: Where it isn't the repository's own dependency, <why> shows which package brings it in.

say.one: <what> comes in through <via>, and its own card already calls for upgrading <planned>. Make that upgrade first, then check for a copy still below <target>, and force one up with <force> only if you find it.
say.many: <what> comes in through <via>, and their own cards already call for upgrading <planned>. Make those upgrades first, then check for a copy still below <target>, and force one up with <force> only if you find it.

say.one: <what> comes in through <via>, and its own card already calls for upgrading <planned>. Make that upgrade first, then run <why> to check for a copy still below <target>, and force one up with <force> only if you find it.
say.many: <what> comes in through <via>, and their own cards already call for upgrading <planned>. Make those upgrades first, then run <why> to check for a copy still below <target>, and force one up with <force> only if you find it.

say.one: <what> comes in through <via>. Upgrade it to a release that uses <name> <target> or later, and if none does yet, force it up with <force>.
say.many: <what> comes in through <via>. Upgrade them to a release that uses <name> <target> or later, and if none does yet, force it up with <force>.

cards.via-breaking.say: Moving from <from> to <target> is a breaking step under semantic versioning, so forcing it can break <parents>. Test before shipping.

cards.unfixed.say: No published version fixes the other <count>, so reduce what reaches <name> or replace it.

cards.rule-unmatched.say: Change the code <where> so the <rule> rule no longer finds it.

cards.history-owned.say: Have a second person review and work on the changes to each main area, name an owner for each in a code owners file, and write down how to build and deploy, so the work doesn't rest on one person.

cards.history-releases.say: Tag each release in git with its version, and release on a regular schedule.

cards.history-dormant.say: Check each named area is still used, remove what isn't, and give each area still in use an owner who keeps it current.

cards.history-slowing.say: Check whether the drop in changes was planned, since an unplanned drop can mean fewer people now work on the code.

cards.history-quiet.say: Check whether anyone still maintains the code. A year with no changes leaves known advisories and fixes unapplied.

cards.history-departed.say: Check that the people still here know the areas the people who left worked on, and write down how those areas work and how to deploy them.

cards.history-tickets.say: Name the ticket or issue each change answers in its commit message.

cards.history-tests.say: Change or add a test in the same commit as each change to the code, and have each review ask for one.

cards.history-reverts.say: Look at why changes were undone. Frequent reverts usually mean changes reach the main branch before anyone has reviewed and tested them.

cards.history-markers.say: Go through the TODO, FIXME, HACK and XXX notes, and finish or remove each one or move it to the issue tracker.

cards.licence-restricted-left.say: Somebody who receives the product could ask for its own source code under these licences' terms. AGPL and SSPL reach even people who only use the product over a network, and a buyer may ask for these dependencies to go before a sale.

cards.licence-restricted-todo.say: Check how the product uses each named dependency. Replace it with one under a permissive licence such as MIT or Apache 2.0, or get legal advice that the product's use doesn't bring the licence's terms into force.

cards.licence-unknown-left.say: A dependency with no licence gives nobody the right to use it, so its author could ask for it to come out of the product.

cards.licence-unknown-todo.say: Find each named dependency's licence where it is published. Where it has none, replace it or get the author's written permission.

cards.licence-in-code-left.say: Code copied into the repository under these licences brings their terms with it. Somebody who receives the product could ask for its source code, and a buyer may ask for that code to go before a sale.

cards.licence-in-code-todo.say: Check where each named file's code came from and how the product uses it. Replace it with code under a permissive licence such as MIT or Apache 2.0, or get legal advice that the product's use doesn't bring the licence's terms into force.
